javascript-toast.heading: JavaScript toast notifications without a framework
javascript-toast.body:
JavaScript toast notifications without a framework

The core of Ding does not need React or Svelte. If you have a plain JavaScript page, a Vue app, or any other setup, you can use the core package directly.

Try it:

Install

npm i @yusufceng1z/ding

Mount and show

import { mountToaster, toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding';

      const unmount = mountToaster({ position: 'top-center' });

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.error('Payment failed', { description: 'Card declined' });

mountToaster returns a function that removes the toaster again, useful if the page is torn down or the toaster should only exist on some routes.

Updating a long task

toast.loading returns an id. Pass it to toast.update to move the same toast through progress and into a result.

const id = toast.loading('Uploading photo…', { progress: 0 });
      toast.update(id, { progress: 0.6 });
      toast.update(id, { type: 'success', title: 'Photo uploaded', progress: null });

Options

Position and theme are set on mountToaster or later with toast.configure({ position, theme }). The full list of options is in the docs.

If you do use React or Svelte, the framework packages are thin wrappers over this one. See React or Svelte. The code is on GitHub.

Position, theme and sound

toast.configure({
  position: 'bottom-right', // top-left, top-center, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-center, bottom-right
  theme: 'dark',            // system, light, dark
  sound: true,
  volume: 0.5,
});

Restyle it with CSS variables

:root .tst-viewport {
  --tst-radius: 8px;
  --tst-bg: #1e3a8a;
  --tst-fg: #fff;
  --tst-success: #16a34a;
}

The playground generates this CSS for you.

Close and clean up

mountToaster returns an unmount function. Call it to remove the toaster. toast.dismiss(id) closes one toast and toast.dismiss() closes all of them.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a framework?

No. @yusufceng1z/ding is plain DOM code with no dependencies. It ships ESM and CommonJS builds.

Is it safe to call during server rendering?

Yes. mountToaster does nothing when there is no document, so it is safe to import and call in code that also runs on the server.

Do I need to import CSS?

No. Styles are injected as one <style> element. If your Content Security Policy blocks inline styles, pass the page's nonce: mountToaster({ nonce }).

Is it accessible?

Yes: live regions, keyboard dismissal and reduced-motion support are built in. See accessible toast notifications.

mainEntity.name: How do I show a loading toast for a promise?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use toast.promise(p, { loading, success, error }). The toast changes to success or error when the promise settles.

mainEntity.name: Does a loading toast close by itself?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Loading toasts stay until you update or dismiss them.

mainEntity.name: Can I show progress?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Pass progress between 0 and 1 and update it with toast.update.

mainEntity.name: What if the request fails?

acceptedAnswer.text: Update the toast to an error, ideally with a Retry button. See undo toast for how an action button can change the toast in place.

loading-toast.heading: Loading toasts: from Saving… to Saved
loading-toast.body:
Loading toasts: from Saving… to Saved

A loading toast says that work started, then becomes the result. The same toast changes from Saving… to Saved. That keeps the result connected to the action that started it.

Try it:

Wrap a promise

This is the shortest version. Pass the promise and the three messages.

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.promise(save(), {
        loading: 'Saving…',
        success: 'Saved',
        error: (err) => `Could not save: ${err.message}`,
      });

Update it by hand

For uploads and other jobs with steps, keep the id and update the toast as you go. progress runs from 0 to 1 and draws a thin bar at the bottom of the toast.

const id = toast.loading('Uploading photo…', { progress: 0 });
      toast.update(id, { progress: 0.6 });
      toast.update(id, { type: 'success', title: 'Photo uploaded', progress: null });

Good to know

A loading toast stays until you update or dismiss it, so make sure every code path ends in one of those. Only the newest caller can update the shared toast. If a slow request finishes after you have shown something newer, its update is ignored instead of overwriting the newer message.

For work that takes minutes, also show progress on the page itself. A toast is a poor place for long-running status. See toast notification UX for when to use which.

Show real progress

Pass progress from 0 to 1 to draw a thin bar at the bottom of the toast, then update it as work advances:

const id = toast.loading('Uploading photo…', { progress: 0 });
toast.update(id, { progress: 0.6 });
toast.update(id, { type: 'success', title: 'Photo uploaded', progress: null });

Why late responses do not overwrite newer messages

Only the newest caller can update the shared toast, so a slow request that finishes late cannot replace a newer message.

Frequently asked questions

How do I show a loading toast for a promise?

Use toast.promise(p, { loading, success, error }). The toast changes to success or error when the promise settles.

Does a loading toast close by itself?

No. Loading toasts stay until you update or dismiss them.

Can I show progress?

Yes. Pass progress between 0 and 1 and update it with toast.update.

What if the request fails?

Update the toast to an error, ideally with a Retry button. See undo toast for how an action button can change the toast in place.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The package ships "use client", so Toaster can go into app/layout.tsx as it is.

mainEntity.name: Can I call toast from a server component or server action?

acceptedAnswer.text: A toast is shown in the browser, so call toast from client code, for example after a server action resolves. The server actions section above shows the pattern.

mainEntity.name: Does it work with a theme switcher?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Pass the current theme to Toaster or call toast.configure({ theme }).

mainEntity.name: Where do I call toast.configure?

acceptedAnswer.text: In an effect inside a client component, not in layout.tsx and not in a component body. A server component gets toast.configure is not a function, and calling it during render gives a React warning about updating Toaster while rendering.

mainEntity.name: Is there a shadcn/ui version?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. npx shadcn@latest add @ding/ding installs the React package and adds a ding-toaster.tsx wrapper. See the shadcn/ui toast guide.

nextjs-toast.heading: Next.js toast notifications
nextjs-toast.body:
Next.js toast notifications

The package is marked "use client", so the Toaster goes straight into your root layout. The one rule: call toast and toast.configure from client code. Everything else is the same as plain React.

Try it:

Install

npm i @yusufceng1z/ding-react

Add the Toaster to the layout

Render it once in app/layout.tsx. The layout stays a server component, no wrapper file needed.

import { Toaster } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
        return (
          <html lang="en">
            <body>
              {children}
              <Toaster position="top-center" theme="system" />
            </body>
          </html>
        );
      }

Configure sound and other options

toast.configure runs in the browser. To set options such as sound, use an effect in a client component that also renders the Toaster:

"use client";

      import { useEffect } from 'react';
      import { Toaster, toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      export function AppToaster() {
        useEffect(() => {
          toast.configure({ sound: true, volume: 0.5 });
        }, []);
        return <Toaster position="top-center" />;
      }

Render <AppToaster /> in app/layout.tsx instead of <Toaster />. Options that Toaster takes as props, such as position, theme, labels and nonce, need no wrapper.

Call toast from client code

"use client";

      import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      export function SaveButton() {
        return <button onClick={() => toast.success('Saved')}>Save</button>;
      }

Server actions

toast runs in the browser, so it cannot be called inside a server action. Call it from the client code that triggers the action and pass the action's promise:

toast.promise(saveAction(formData), {
        loading: 'Saving…',
        success: 'Saved',
        error: 'Could not save',
      });

With the Pages Router, render <Toaster /> in pages/_app.tsx. If the project uses shadcn/ui, the shadcn install also works. For the non-Next parts see React toast notifications.

Theme and styling

Ding follows the system theme by default. If your site has its own theme switch, such as a .dark class, pass the current theme to the toaster:

<Toaster theme={theme} position="top-center" />

Colors and corner radius are CSS variables, so a global stylesheet is enough to match your design:

:root .tst-viewport {
  --tst-radius: 8px;
  --tst-bg: #1e3a8a;
  --tst-fg: #fff;
  --tst-success: #16a34a;
}

Content Security Policy

Styles are injected as one <style> element. If your CSP blocks inline styles, pass the request nonce with <Toaster nonce={nonce} />. Per-toast values are set through the DOM, so only the stylesheet needs the nonce.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a client component wrapper?

No. The package ships "use client", so Toaster can go into app/layout.tsx as it is.

Can I call toast from a server component or server action?

A toast is shown in the browser, so call toast from client code, for example after a server action resolves. The server actions section above shows the pattern.

Does it work with a theme switcher?

Yes. Pass the current theme to Toaster or call toast.configure({ theme }).

Where do I call toast.configure?

In an effect inside a client component. The layout can stay a server component. See the example above.

Is there a shadcn/ui version?

Yes. npx shadcn@latest add @ding/ding installs the React package and adds a ding-toaster.tsx wrapper. See the shadcn/ui toast guide.

react-hot-toast-alternative.heading: A react-hot-toast alternative
react-hot-toast-alternative.body:
A react-hot-toast alternative

react-hot-toast has a small, friendly API, and Ding keeps that feel. Ding morphs quick notifications in place. Action and error toasts have their own slots in the default held mode.

Try it:

Same kind of API

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.error('Payment failed');
      toast.promise(save(), { loading: 'Saving…', success: 'Saved', error: 'Failed' });

Render <Toaster /> once near the root, the same way you do today.

What changes

A second quick call changes the current quick message in place. You can also update a toast yourself with toast.update(id, patch), which makes progress bars and multi-step jobs easy, and sound is available if you want it (off by default).

Ding also ships a Svelte 5 package and a framework-free one, in case you work in more than one stack.

Install

npm i @yusufceng1z/ding-react

Full setup is on the React toast page, and a comparison with a stacking alternative is on the Sonner page.

The same calls, side by side

Taskreact-hot-toastDing
Importreact-hot-toast@yusufceng1z/ding-react
Render once<Toaster /><Toaster />
Successtoast.success('Saved')toast.success('Saved')
Promisetoast.promise(p, {...})toast.promise(p, {...})
Dismisstoast.dismiss(id)toast.dismiss(id)

For these everyday calls, switching is mostly a change of import. Options and custom rendering differ, so check yours against the docs.

What you get in return

  • Spring-based motion that keeps its momentum when interrupted.
  • A toast that changes in place, from loading to success or error.
  • No stylesheet to import and no dependencies.
  • Svelte 5, Vue 3 and plain JavaScript versions, not only React.

Frequently asked questions

Is Ding a drop-in replacement for react-hot-toast?

For toast.success, toast.error, toast.promise and toast.dismiss the call shape is the same. Other options differ, so test the ones you use.

Does Ding need a stylesheet?

No. Styles are injected from JavaScript.

Can I restyle the toast?

Yes. Colors and corner radius are CSS variables, and the playground generates the CSS for you.

Does it work in the Next.js App Router?

Yes. See the Next.js toast guide.

react-toast.heading: React toast notifications
react-toast.body:
React toast notifications

Ding is a React toast library with no dependencies and no stylesheet. You render one component and call a function. This page covers the setup and the parts people usually ask about next.

Try it:

Install

One package, nothing else to add.

npm i @yusufceng1z/ding-react

Render the Toaster once

Put it near the root of the app. The styles are injected from JavaScript, so there is no CSS file to import.

import { Toaster } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      export default function App() {
        return (
          <>
            <Toaster position="top-center" theme="system" />
            {/* your app */}
          </>
        );
      }

Call toast from anywhere

toast is a plain function, so it works in event handlers, effects, data-fetching code and anything else that is not a component.

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.error('Payment failed', { description: 'Card declined' });

A new quick toast replaces the content of the quick toast already on screen. Errors and other held toasts keep their place by default. See held toasts for the other modes. Calling it with the same message twice adds a counter (×2) instead of a second toast.

Saving, loading and undo

For a request, pass the promise and one toast goes from loading to the result. The loading toast page has the details.

toast.promise(save(), {
        loading: 'Saving…',
        success: 'Saved',
        error: (err) => `Could not save: ${err.message}`,
      });

An action button can return a patch, which is how undo toasts confirm that the undo worked.

Next.js and shadcn/ui

The package is marked "use client", so in the Next.js App Router Toaster can go straight into a server layout. The Next.js setup shows how. If the project uses shadcn/ui, there is also a one-command install.

Timing

Plain toasts close after 5 seconds. Errors, loading toasts and toasts with a button stay until the user dismisses them, because those are the ones people must not miss. Hover, keyboard focus and a hidden tab pause the countdown.

I wrote Ding because I wanted a toast that does not pile up. If that sounds like what you need, a star on GitHub helps others find it.

Position, theme and sound

The toaster takes its settings as props, and the same settings work from anywhere with toast.configure:

<Toaster position="bottom-right" theme="dark" />

toast.configure({ sound: true, volume: 0.5 });

There are six positions (top and bottom, each left, center or right) and three themes: system, light and dark. The toaster mirrors itself on right-to-left pages.

Restyle it with CSS variables

Colors and corner radius are CSS variables, so you can match your design system without touching the library:

:root .tst-viewport {
  --tst-radius: 8px;
  --tst-bg: #1e3a8a;
  --tst-fg: #fff;
  --tst-success: #16a34a;
}

Read the CSS variables guide or try the options live in the playground, which also gives you the CSS to copy.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to import a CSS file?

No. Ding injects its styles from JavaScript, so there is nothing to import. If your Content Security Policy blocks inline styles, pass the page's nonce with <Toaster nonce={nonce} />.

Which React versions does Ding support?

React 18 and newer, through @yusufceng1z/ding-react.

Does Ding work with the Next.js App Router?

Yes. The package ships "use client", so Toaster can go straight into app/layout.tsx. See the Next.js toast guide.

Does Ding have dependencies?

No third-party dependencies. The React package renders on top of the small Ding core.

How do I update a toast instead of showing a new one?

Keep the id that toast.loading returns and call toast.update(id, { type: 'success', title: 'Saved' }), or wrap a promise with toast.promise.

shadcn-toast.heading: A shadcn/ui toast you can add with the CLI
shadcn-toast.body:
A shadcn/ui toast you can add with the CLI

Ding publishes a registry item, so the shadcn CLI can install it like any other component.

Try it:

Add it

npx shadcn@latest add @ding/ding

Ding is listed in the shadcn registry directory, so the @ding namespace works without any setup. The full URL works too: npx shadcn@latest add https://ding.yusufcengiz.dev/r/ding.json.

This installs @yusufceng1z/ding-react and writes components/ding-toaster.tsx. The file is tiny: it re-exports the Toaster as DingToaster, plus toast, and marks itself "use client" so it works in the Next.js App Router.

Use it

import { DingToaster } from '@/components/ding-toaster';

      // once, in your root layout
      <DingToaster position="top-center" />
import { toast } from '@/components/ding-toaster';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.error('Payment failed', { description: 'Card declined' });

How it differs from the stock shadcn toast

Ding morphs quick notifications when you call again and keeps held toasts visible by default. The styles come from JavaScript, so it does not depend on Tailwind or add CSS to your project. Use a stacking pattern if your app needs every quick message visible at the same time.

Not on shadcn? The same package works anywhere, see React toast notifications.

Match your shadcn theme

Ding's colors and corner radius are CSS variables. Point them at your own theme tokens, for example when your tokens hold full colors:

:root .tst-viewport {
  --tst-bg: var(--popover);
  --tst-fg: var(--popover-foreground);
  --tst-radius: var(--radius);
}

If your site switches themes with a class, pass the current theme to the toaster so the two stay in sync.

sonner-alternative.heading: Ding as a Sonner alternative
sonner-alternative.body:
Ding as a Sonner alternative

Sonner is a good library and it stacks toasts. Ding makes a different choice: a quick toast morphs when the next quick message arrives, while persistent notifications keep their place. Which you want depends on your app.

Try it:

Why I made one toast at a time

In the apps I work on, a burst of events (save, then sync, then a failed request) produced a stack that covered the page and was harder to read than a single message. I wanted the latest message to win, with a visible transition so the user sees that it changed.

Pick Ding if

You want one message at a time. You update the same toast through loading, success and undo. You want zero dependencies and no CSS import. Or you use Svelte 5 or plain JavaScript as well as React.

Pick Sonner if

Choose Sonner if you want every quick notification to get its own slot. Ding supports multiple held notifications and keeps quick feedback in a single slot.

Switching

The calls look familiar. Render one Toaster, then:

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.promise(save(), { loading: 'Saving…', success: 'Saved', error: 'Failed' });

Check the options you use against the docs before swapping, since not every option exists. Setup details are in React toast notifications. If you use Svelte, see the svelte-sonner alternative.

Ding is open source on GitHub. A star is the easiest way to say it was useful.

What Ding brings

  • Springs, not fades. Size, shape and text move on a spring solver, so interrupting an animation keeps its momentum.
  • No stylesheet and no dependencies. Styles are injected from JavaScript.
  • Four renderers. React, Svelte 5, Vue 3 and plain JavaScript share one core.
  • Rich content. Description, avatar, buttons, a progress bar, a countdown line and small trailing text.
  • Easy restyling. Colors and corner radius are CSS variables.

API at a glance

TaskDing
Render once<Toaster />
Show a messagetoast.success('Saved'), error, warning, info, loading
Wrap a promisetoast.promise(p, { loading, success, error })
Change a toasttoast.update(id, patch)
Closetoast.dismiss(id) or toast.dismiss()

Is Ding a drop-in replacement for Sonner?

The common calls look alike, but not every option exists in both libraries. Check the options you use against the docs before swapping.

Does Ding work outside React?

Yes. There are packages for Svelte 5 and Vue 3, and a plain JavaScript version. See svelte-sonner alternative and JavaScript toast notifications.

Does Ding need a CSS import?

No. Styles are injected from JavaScript.

Can I use Ding with shadcn/ui?

Yes, with one command. See the shadcn/ui toast guide.

A svelte-sonner alternative for Svelte 5

svelte-sonner is a Svelte port of Sonner and it stacks toasts. Ding morphs quick toasts in place and keeps persistent toasts visible by default.

        import { Toaster } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-svelte';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.promise(save(), { loading: 'Saving…', success: 'Saved', error: 'Failed' });

The full Svelte setup is on the Svelte toast page, and the reasoning behind one toast at a time is on the Sonner alternative page.

svelte-toast.heading: Svelte 5 toast notifications
svelte-toast.body:
Svelte 5 toast notifications

Ding has a Svelte package built for Svelte 5. It has no dependencies, needs no stylesheet, and the toast function works from components and from plain modules.

Try it:

Install

npm i @yusufceng1z/ding-svelte

It targets Svelte 5 only. If you are still on Svelte 4, this package will not work for you.

Mount it in the root layout

In SvelteKit that is src/routes/+layout.svelte. In a plain Svelte app, use your top-level component.

<script>
        import { Toaster } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-svelte';
        let { children } = $props();
      </script>

      {@render children()}
      <Toaster position="top-center" theme="system" />

Show a toast

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-svelte';

      toast.success('Saved');
      toast.error('Payment failed', { description: 'Card declined' });

You can call it from a +page.ts load function, a store, an event handler, anywhere that runs in the browser. Call it on the server and nothing happens, since there is no page to show it on.

Behavior to know about

New quick toasts morph the current quick notification. Errors and action toasts stay visible by default until dismissed. That is the main difference from stacking libraries such as svelte-sonner, which I compare on the svelte-sonner alternative page.

Errors, loading toasts and toasts that have a button stay until dismissed. Everything else closes after five seconds. For loading states see loading toast, and for undo buttons see undo toast.

Position, theme and sound

Set them as props on Toaster, or call toast.configure from anywhere:

<Toaster position="bottom-right" theme="dark" />

toast.configure({ sound: true, volume: 0.5 });

Restyle it with CSS variables

Colors and corner radius are CSS variables, so they work the same in Svelte as in any other framework:

:root .tst-viewport {
  --tst-radius: 8px;
  --tst-bg: #1e3a8a;
  --tst-fg: #fff;
  --tst-success: #16a34a;
}

toast-accessibility.heading: Making toast notifications accessible
toast-accessibility.body:
Making toast notifications accessible

A toast that a screen reader never announces, or that disappears before a keyboard user can reach its button, does not work. These are the four things to check.

Announce it

Put the text in a live region so screen readers read it without moving focus. role="status" is polite and fits most messages. role="alert" interrupts, so keep it for urgent errors. Ding announces errors assertively and everything else politely. Live-region support varies between screen readers, so test with the ones your users have.

Give people time

A message on a timer is a problem for anyone who reads slowly or needs longer to react. Pause the timer on hover and on keyboard focus, keep toasts with buttons on screen longer, and do not auto-dismiss errors. In Ding, errors, loading toasts and toasts with a button stay until dismissed.

Keyboard access

If a toast has a button, keyboard users need a way to reach it. In Ding, Alt + T moves focus into the toast and Esc dismisses it.

Reduced motion

Spring animation looks good and some people turn motion off. Ding follows prefers-reduced-motion.

What a library cannot do for you

Do not let a toast be the only place a critical message or an Undo lives. Keep the text short and plain. See toast notification UX for when a toast is the right choice, and undo toast for a pattern that needs a second way back.

Which WCAG criteria apply

  • 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA): a message must be announced without taking focus, which is what a live region does.
  • 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (A): if content disappears on a timer, people need a way to extend or stop it.
  • 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A): anything that moves or updates on its own for more than five seconds needs a way to pause it.
  • 1.4.1 Use of Color (A): status needs a second cue, such as an icon or text.

What Ding does for you

  • Messages go through persistent live regions: errors are assertive, everything else is polite.
  • Esc dismisses. It does nothing while a dialog, menu or text field has focus, so it does not steal the key.
  • Alt + T moves focus into the toast.
  • Hover, keyboard focus and a hidden tab pause the countdown. Errors, loading toasts and toasts with a button stay until dismissed.
  • Motion respects prefers-reduced-motion, and the toaster mirrors on right-to-left pages.
  • The region and close button names can be localized with the labels option.

Frequently asked questions

Should a toast take keyboard focus?

Usually not, because it would interrupt what the user is doing. Announce it through a live region and offer a shortcut, such as Alt + T in Ding, to reach it.

Is role=alert right for every toast?

No. alert is assertive and interrupts the screen reader. Use it for errors and a polite status region for everything else.

How long should a toast stay?

Long enough to read it, and anything with a button should wait for the user. See toast notification UX.

Can I translate the labels?

Yes. Pass labels to toast.configure or to Toaster: region and dismiss keep their English defaults unless you set them.

toast-notification-ux.heading: Toast notification UX: when a toast is the right tool
toast-notification-ux.body:
Toast notification UX: when a toast is the right tool

A toast is a short message that shows up after something happened and leaves by itself. That makes it good for small confirmations and bad for anything a person has to see.

Good uses

Confirm something the user just did: saved, copied, sent. Offer a quick way back, like Undo after a delete. Report that background work finished, for example an export that was running while the user did something else.

Bad uses

Errors the user has to fix belong next to the field that failed, where they stay visible. Anything critical, legal or about money should not disappear after a few seconds. And a toast is one sentence with at most one button. If you need a paragraph or two choices, use a dialog or an inline message.

How long it should stay

Five seconds is a reasonable default for a short sentence. A toast with a button needs longer, because the person has to notice it and then move to it. Hover and keyboard focus should pause the timer so reading is never a race. In Ding, errors, loading toasts and toasts with a button do not time out at all.

One toast or a stack

A stack keeps history but covers the page when many things happen quickly. A single toast that changes in place keeps attention on the latest message and loses the older ones. Ding uses that approach for quick updates and gives held notifications their own slots by default. If each urgent notification needs an action, keep those messages visible.

Wording

Say what happened in a few words: Saved, Link copied. For an error say what failed and what to try: Could not save. Check your connection and try again. Leave out exclamation marks and the word successfully, they add length and no information.

Two related pages: the undo pattern and making toasts accessible. If you are choosing a name or a library, see toast vs snackbar.

A quick checklist

  • The message is short and says what happened.
  • Nothing the user must act on lives only in a toast. Errors that block work need a place that stays.
  • Color is never the only signal. Pair it with an icon or words.
  • An error says what to do next, or offers a Retry button.
  • The toast can be dismissed, and it waits while the user is reading or interacting with it.
  • Motion respects prefers-reduced-motion.

What Ding does by default

Ding closes a toast after 5000 ms. Errors, loading toasts and toasts with a button stay until dismissed. Hover, keyboard focus and a hidden tab pause the countdown, and you can set duration per toast. See the accessibility guide for the reasoning behind timing.

Frequently asked questions

How long should a toast stay on screen?

Long enough to read the message, which is a few seconds for a short one. Anything that needs a decision or action should wait for the user instead of timing out.

When should I not use a toast?

For form validation errors, which belong next to the field, and for anything the user must not miss. A toast disappears, so it is a poor home for required information.

Should a toast have an undo button?

Often yes, for reversible actions that people take often. See how to build an undo toast.

Toast or snackbar?

The names mostly overlap. Toast vs snackbar explains where people draw a line.

toast-vs-snackbar.heading: Toast vs snackbar
toast-vs-snackbar.body:
Toast vs snackbar

Mostly no. Both words describe a short message that appears over the page, then goes away on its own. The difference is mainly which design tradition you learned the word from.

Where the names come from

Toast is the common word on the web and in a lot of component libraries, named after bread popping out of a toaster. Snackbar is the term Material Design uses, and libraries built on Material follow it.

Where people draw a line

Some teams use snackbar for a single message fixed to a screen edge, usually with one action, and toast for any floating message including ones that stack. That is a team convention, not a standard. If your design system already picked a word, use it everywhere, in code, docs and conversation.

What to actually decide

The name matters less than the behavior. Decide whether messages stack or replace each other, where they appear, how long they stay, and whether they can carry an action. Ding is a toast library that shows one message at a time and replaces it on the next call. The UX guide goes through those choices.

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.success('Saved');

A short comparison

ToastSnackbar
Origin of the namePops up like toast from a toaster. Android also has a system Toast class.Material Design component.
Typical contentA short messageA short message with at most one action
PositionAnywhere on screenUsually at the bottom

In web UI the two words are often used for the same thing, so decide by behavior: how long it stays, whether it has an action and whether it can be dismissed.

Is a snackbar the same as a toast?

Mostly. Both are brief messages that appear over the page and go away. A snackbar is the Material Design name and usually carries one action.

Can a toast have a button?

Yes. Ding supports a main action and a quieter secondary button. A toast with a button stays until dismissed. See undo toast.

Which should I use in React?

Either name describes the same component. Install Ding in React and you get both behaviors.

undo-toast.heading: How to build an undo toast
undo-toast.body:
How to build an undo toast

A confirm dialog before every delete slows people down and they click through it anyway. Doing the action and offering Undo in a toast is faster, and safer if the undo actually works.

Try it:

The code

import { toast } from '@yusufceng1z/ding-react';

      toast.success('Message deleted', {
        action: {
          label: 'Undo',
          onClick: () => {
            restore();
            return { type: 'info', title: 'Restored' };
          },
        },
      });

The click handler may return a patch. When it does, the toast changes in place to Restored instead of closing, so the person gets confirmation that the undo worked. The same code works with @yusufceng1z/ding-svelte and @yusufceng1z/ding, only the import differs.

Making the undo real

Do not delete for good when the button is shown. Mark the item as deleted first, and remove it only after the undo window has passed, or never, if you keep a trash. Otherwise Undo is a promise you cannot keep when the request has already finished.

A toast with a button stays until dismissed in Ding, so nobody is racing a timer. Still, keep a second way back, such as a trash view. A toast is easy to miss, and for some people it is hard to reach, see toast accessibility.

More on when toasts are the right tool: toast notification UX.

Morph the toast after Undo

An onClick can return a patch. The toast then changes in place instead of closing, so the user sees that the undo worked:

toast.success('Message deleted', {
  action: {
    label: 'Undo',
    onClick: () => {
      restore();
      return { type: 'info', title: 'Restored' };
    },
  },
});

Give the undo a time limit

A toast with a button stays until dismissed. Set duration to close it after a time limit, and a thin countdown line shows how long is left:

toast.success('Message deleted', {
  duration: 8000,
  action: { label: 'Undo', onClick: restore },
});

Frequently asked questions

Why use undo instead of a confirmation dialog?

People confirm out of habit. Doing the action at once and offering undo is faster, and a mistake is still easy to reverse.

How long should the undo window be?

Long enough to notice and react, often several seconds. Set it with duration. Hover, keyboard focus and a hidden tab pause the countdown.

Can the toast change after the user clicks Undo?

Yes. Return a patch from onClick, for example { type: 'info', title: 'Restored' }.

When is undo not enough?

For actions that cannot be reversed or that affect other people, ask first. See toast notification UX.
